--- title: "Estimating EIR from prevalence" --- A parasite survey gives a prevalence, and the transmission model needs an EIR. `estimint` inverts the one into the other and returns the EIR that would have sustained the measured prevalence. Prevalence alone is not enough. Six covariates describing the setting go in alongside it. ## The prevalence model Load the model by name. It ships inside the wheel, so the call is offline and takes milliseconds. ::: {#5e95fbff .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from estimint import load_xgb_model, run_xgb_model prev_model = load_xgb_model("prevalence") prev_model["features"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['dn0_use', 'Q0', 'phi_bednets', 'seasonal', 'itn_use', 'irs_use', 'prev_y9'] ``` ::: ::: All seven columns are required. Six describe the setting, and the seventh, `prev_y9`, carries the driving input. | Column | Meaning | |---|---| | `dn0_use` | Probability a mosquito dies on contact with a net. From `calculate_dn0`. | | `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1 | | `phi_bednets` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed | | `seasonal` | 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal | | `itn_use` | ITN coverage, 0 to 1. From `calculate_dn0`. | | `irs_use` | IRS coverage, 0 to 1 | | `prev_y9` | Parasite prevalence in the deployment year, 0 to 1 | A missing column raises a `ValueError` naming it. `prevalence` is accepted as an alias for `prev_y9` and copied across, which is convenient, because `estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta` expects that name too. `run_xgb_model` takes the frame and the model and returns a plain NumPy array, one element per row. ::: {#51aae0cb .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} setting = dict( dn0_use=0.33, Q0=0.87, phi_bednets=0.82, seasonal=0.0, itn_use=0.6, irs_use=0.0, ) one = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": 0.30}]) eir = run_xgb_model(one, prev_model) type(eir), eir ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (numpy.ndarray, array([13.39696895])) ``` ::: ::: A prevalence of 30% in this setting implies about 13.4 infectious bites per person per year. ## Sweeping prevalence Sweeping the prevalence with the setting held fixed shows that the EIR is nowhere near linear in it, and that doubling prevalence from 0.30 to 0.60 raises the EIR roughly fivefold rather than doubling it. Between 0.60 and 0.75 it more than doubles again. ::: {#82c73871 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} sweep = pd.DataFrame( [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75]] ) sweep["eir"] = run_xgb_model(sweep, prev_model) sweep[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
prevalence eir
0 0.05 1.47
1 0.10 2.87
2 0.20 6.79
3 0.30 13.40
4 0.45 28.82
5 0.60 64.22
6 0.75 158.88
``` ::: ::: ::: {#06f76e3c .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np grid = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in np.linspace(0.05, 0.75, 71)]) grid["eir"] = run_xgb_model(grid, prev_model) fig, ax = plt.subplots() ax.plot(grid["prevalence"], grid["eir"], color="#00d4aa") ax.set_xlabel("Prevalence") ax.set_ylabel("EIR (infectious bites per person per year)") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Inferred EIR against prevalence, holding the setting fixed.](estimating-eir_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){fig-alt='A teal line rising slowly from near zero at 5% prevalence then climbing very steeply above 60% prevalence, reaching about 160 infectious bites per person per year at 75%.'} ::: ::: The teal curve is nearly flat below a prevalence of 0.3 and climbs almost vertically above 0.6. This is because prevalence saturates while transmission does not, so once most of the population already carries parasites, a further rise in prevalence can only come from a very large rise in the bites behind it. An input a few points out at 70% therefore moves the inferred EIR by tens of bites per year, while the same error at 20% moves it by less than one. ## The role of the setting The same measured prevalence implies different EIRs in different settings, and net coverage is the covariate that moves the answer most. The district in the running example has a prevalence of 0.45, pyrethroid resistance of 0.30, and pyrethroid-only nets. Only the coverage varies below. ::: {#146818e0 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import calculate_dn0 rows = [] for coverage in [0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]: nets = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=coverage) rows.append({ "coverage": coverage, "dn0_use": nets.dn0, "itn_use": nets.itn_use, "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0.0, "irs_use": 0.0, "prevalence": 0.45, }) nets_vs_eir = pd.DataFrame(rows) nets_vs_eir["eir"] = run_xgb_model(nets_vs_eir, prev_model) nets_vs_eir[["coverage", "dn0_use", "itn_use", "prevalence", "eir"]].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
coverage dn0_use itn_use prevalence eir
0 0.0 0.000 0.0 0.45 22.536
1 0.3 0.311 0.3 0.45 24.170
2 0.5 0.311 0.5 0.45 26.461
3 0.7 0.311 0.7 0.45 31.960
4 0.9 0.311 0.9 0.45 37.058
``` ::: ::: Every row reports the same prevalence, and the inferred EIR still rises by roughly two thirds down the column. This is because a district that holds 45% prevalence under 90% net coverage must be absorbing far more infectious bites than one that holds the same prevalence with no nets at all. The nets have already suppressed a large share of them. Understating `itn_use`, the error described in [Nets and dn0](nets-and-dn0.qmd), therefore biases the EIR downwards. ## The global model `set_global_model` registers a model as the default, after which `run_xgb_model` may be called with the frame alone, and `get_global_model` returns whatever is currently registered. ::: {#151ae7d4 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} from estimint import set_global_model, get_global_model set_global_model(prev_model) run_xgb_model(one) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` array([13.39696895]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#204d42e5 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} get_global_model()["class"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` 'estiMINT_model' ``` ::: ::: Note that the global slot holds exactly one model. Pass it explicitly in any script that touches more than one of the three, because a stray `set_global_model` elsewhere changes what an unqualified call resolves to. ::: {.callout-note} ## The valid range `prev_y9` is clamped to `[0.005, 0.80]`, and values outside that band are quietly pulled to the nearest edge. No warning is raised. ::: {#0b21a424 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} edges = pd.DataFrame( [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.001, 0.005, 0.80, 0.95]] ) edges["eir"] = run_xgb_model(edges, prev_model) edges[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
prevalence eir
0 0.001 0.894
1 0.005 0.894
2 0.800 234.882
3 0.950 234.882
``` ::: ::: Note that a prevalence of 0.001 and one of 0.005 return the same EIR, as do 0.80 and 0.95, and that a sweep producing an implausibly flat EIR at either end has almost always hit this clamp. The epidemiology is rarely the cause. ::: ## See also The same inversion runs from entomological data where there is no parasite survey, and [EIR and HBR](eir-and-hbr.qmd) works through both directions of it. Please see [Mosquito density and EIR](mosquito-density.qmd) for the EIR when the vector population changes.
